title: Giant Exfoliation Induced Magnetic Coercivity in Fe$_3$GaTe$_2$
authors: Lingrui Mei, PeiYu Cai, Sang-Eon Lee, Yue Li, Shyam Raj Karullithodi, Vadym Kulichenko, Charudatta Pathak, Elton J. G. Santos, Luis Balicas
abstract: Permanent magnets with strong anisotropy and high coercivity underpin modern information and energy technologies, yet rare-earth-free alternatives remain limited. Here, we show that thickness engineering via mechanical exfoliation induces hard magnetic behavior in the van der Waals ferromagnet Fe$_3$GaTe$_2$. Bulk crystals exhibit Curie temperatures above 350 K but negligible room-temperature coercivity. When thinned below 100 nm, the coercive field is dramatically enhanced, reaching nearly 1 T at room temperature for in-plane fields which is comparable to values of conventional hard magnets. Micromagnetic analysis reveals a crossover in magnetization reversal from domain-mediated processes in bulk samples to quasi-coherent rotation in thin flakes, driven by increased effective anisotropy and suppressed domain formation. This thickness-dependent transition enables tuning of magnetic hardness without chemical modification. Combined with high saturation magnetization and robust room-temperature performance, Fe$_3$GaTe$_2$ emerges as a promising rare-earth-free material for spintronic applications. Its layered structure further allows integration into van der Waals heterostructures, where large in-plane coercivity can stabilize magnetic states against perturbations and interlayer coupling, offering potential for high-density nonvolatile memory and domain-wall-based devices.
summary: This work demonstrates that mechanically exfoliating the van der Waals ferromagnet $	ext{Fe}_3	ext{GaTe}_2$ induces a giant enhancement in its room-temperature magnetic coercivity. This effect is attributed to the transition from multi-domain behavior in bulk crystals to quasi-coherent, single-domain rotation in thin flakes. The findings position $	ext{Fe}_3	ext{GaTe}_2$ as a highly promising, rare-earth-free material for next-generation spintronic memory devices.
main_problem: The primary goal is to develop rare-earth-free permanent magnets with high coercivity for spintronic applications, overcoming the limitations of bulk materials.
main_result: Mechanical exfoliation dramatically enhances the room-temperature coercive field in $	ext{Fe}_3	ext{GaTe}_2$ from negligible values to nearly 1 T when the field is applied in the plane.
method: The study combines experimental measurements (magnetization, anomalous Hall effect) on exfoliated flakes with micromagnetic simulations to analyze the magnetic reversal mechanism.
model_or_system: The system is $	ext{Fe}_3	ext{GaTe}_2$, a van der Waals ferromagnet. The analysis uses the Stoner-Wohlfarth model and micromagnetic theory to describe magnetization reversal, contrasting bulk domain-mediated behavior with thin-flake quasi-coherent rotation.
key_observables: Coercive field ($\mu_0H_c$), saturation magnetization ($M_s$), Anomalous Hall resistivity ($ho_{xy}^A$), and magnetic anisotropy constant ($K$).
important_parameters: Thickness (down to $<100 	ext{ nm}$), temperature ($2 	ext{ K}$ to $300 	ext{ K}$), and field orientation relative to the crystal planes.
main_assumptions: The enhancement in coercivity is attributed to the system approaching a single-domain limit, governed by intrinsic magnetocrystalline anisotropy, rather than disorder-induced pinning mechanisms.
figures_summary: Figures show $\mu_0H_c$ increasing significantly for planar fields compared to c-axis fields upon exfoliation. Anomalous Hall response plots are used to analyze thickness dependence and distinguish intrinsic vs. extrinsic magnetic contributions.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the need for rare-earth-free magnets, presents experimental evidence showing coercivity enhancement via exfoliation (comparing bulk vs. thin flakes), analyzes this using micromagnetics/AHE measurements, and concludes that the material is promising for spintronics due to its tunable planar anisotropy.
why_interesting: While primarily condensed matter magnetism, the study of thickness-dependent magnetic transitions and the use of van der Waals heterostructures touches upon concepts relevant to engineered quantum interfaces and low-dimensional physics.
